contests.title: Proposition A — Charter Changes Affecting Various City Departments and Commissions
contests.summary: Updates the City Charter to reflect current department operations, changes procedures, and eliminates or reorganizes some commissions and advisory bodies. It also requires supervisors to amend certain voter-approved laws to carry out these changes.

contests.title: Proposition B — Establishing a Municipal Finance Corporation and a Public Bank
contests.summary: Allows the City to create a lending corporation if funding and resources are sufficient; after three years it may become a public bank that also takes deposits. It authorizes these institutions but does not require their creation.

contests.title: Proposition C — Contributions to the Housing Trust Fund
contests.summary: Changes the formula for City housing contributions, increases funding and expands eligible housing programs, and extends the fund from 2043 to 2058. Annual funding increases could be frozen, or contributions reduced, under specified budget conditions.

contests.title: Proposition D — Changes to Ballot Measure Process
contests.shortTitle: Rules for putting measures on the ballot
contests.summary: Raises the initiative petition threshold from 2% to 8% of registered voters and increases special-election requirements, while allowing initiatives to be withdrawn. The Mayor or a minority of supervisors could no longer place measures on the ballot independently; a Board majority still could.

contests.title: Proposition E — City Administrator’s Authority and Changes to City Contracting
contests.summary: Centralizes purchasing authority under the City Administrator, raises contract values requiring supervisors’ approval, and extends the administrator’s term from five to ten years. Supervisors and the Mayor could approve or reject proposed purchasing rules but generally not amend them; proposals take effect after 60 days without action.

contests.title: Proposition F — Changes to Executive Branch Management
contests.summary: Expands the Mayor’s authority to move department responsibilities unless the Board objects, hire deputy mayors, and hire some or fire most department heads, with specified exceptions. Appointing officials could remove most commissioners without cause.

contests.title: Proposition G — Allowing Private Vehicles on the Upper Great Highway in Sunset Dunes Park
contests.shortTitle: Weekday cars on the Great Highway
contests.summary: Closes Sunset Dunes Park from Monday at 4 a.m. to Friday at 6 p.m., except weekday holidays, to reopen the Upper Great Highway to private vehicles. Reopening would require the necessary government approvals and permits.

contests.title: Proposition H — Parcel Tax to Fund Muni Operations
contests.summary: Creates a 15-year annual property parcel tax for Muni starting July 2027, with rates based on property type and size and adjusted for inflation. Single-family homes start at $129 per year; exemptions and senior discounts apply, and the largest parcels can owe up to $400,000.

contests.title: Proposition I — Changes to Real Property Transfer Tax
contests.summary: Redirects half of the transfer tax on qualifying real-estate sales of $10 million or more to affordable housing and housing assistance, without raising current combined rates. It exempts certain first sales of newly built multifamily housing from the dedicated portion.

contests.title: Proposition J — Removal of Foreclosure Exemption for Real Property Transfer Tax
contests.summary: Taxes the full market value of certain properties transferred to lenders through foreclosure or to avoid foreclosure, starting March 2027. Existing relief remains for single-family homes, residential buildings with fewer than five units, and qualifying small mixed-use properties.

contests.title: Regional Transit Measure
contests.summary: Adds a 1% sales tax in San Francisco and 0.5% in Alameda, Contra Costa, San Mateo and Santa Clara counties for 14 years. Revenue funds transit and related programs; passage depends on the combined vote across all five counties.

contests.title: Proposition 1 — Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs
contests.summary: Allows $11.25 billion in state borrowing for affordable housing, veterans’ mortgages and homeownership assistance. State repayment costs are estimated at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years.

contests.title: Proposition 2 — Increases State’s Rainy Day Fund
contests.summary: Raises the rainy-day fund target from 10% to 20% of General Fund taxes and requires larger deposits when investment-gains tax revenue is very high. It extends extra debt payments through 2040 and counts reserve money toward the state spending limit when withdrawn rather than deposited.

contests.title: Proposition 3 — Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
contests.summary: Makes existing higher tax rates on high incomes permanent instead of allowing them to expire in 2031. The measure supports schools and community colleges and makes more General Fund revenue available for health care and other programs.

contests.title: Proposition 4 — Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns
contests.summary: Lets state and local governments create public campaign-funding programs for eligible candidates who accept spending limits. It bars using money earmarked for education, transportation or public safety and triples the maximum fine for foreign campaign contributions.

contests.title: Proposition 5 — Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers
contests.summary: Removes the replacement-candidate election from the recall ballot: a recalled governor would be succeeded by the lieutenant governor. Other recalled offices would be filled later by election or appointment under existing law; a recalled official could run in a later special election.

contests.title: Proposition 37 — Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New Homes
contests.shortTitle: Loans for buyers of new homes
contests.summary: Authorizes up to $25 billion in bonds for loans covering up to 17% of a qualifying new home’s price, repaid through borrowers’ mortgage payments. Buyers must meet residency, occupancy, income and down-payment requirements, and homes must meet price limits.

contests.title: Proposition 38 — Authorizes Bonds for Immunology Medical Research
contests.summary: Allows $8.4 billion in state borrowing for immune-system research and treatments, with at least half directed to cancer, heart disease and Alzheimer’s disease. Estimated repayment is $500 million to $600 million annually for about 20 years, potentially offset by research revenue.

contests.title: Proposition 39 — Prohibits Citizens from Voting Unless They Present Government-Issued Identification
contests.summary: Requires government-issued ID for in-person voting and the last four digits of the ID number selected in a voter’s registration on mail-ballot envelopes. It provides free voter ID cards on request and requires officials to make best efforts to verify voters’ citizenship and report annually.

contests.title: Proposition 40 — Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers
contests.summary: Imposes a one-time tax of up to 5% on covered assets of certain billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026, excluding real estate and some retirement assets. It directs 90% of revenue to health care and the rest to education, food assistance and administering the tax.

contests.title: Proposition 41 — Prohibits New State Taxes that Exclude Revenues from State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes
contests.shortTitle: State tax spending limits and audits
contests.summary: Bars new state taxes that exclude their revenue from the state spending limit and requires audits before and after certain new or increased state special taxes are approved. It could override conflicting measures on this ballot if it receives more Yes votes.

contests.title: Proposition 42 — Prohibits New State Personal Property Taxes and Certain Retroactive State Taxes
contests.shortTitle: Limits on property and retroactive taxes
contests.summary: Bans new state taxes on personal property, including financial assets, and certain taxes based on conduct or status before the tax takes effect. It applies to taxes enacted or taking effect from January 1, 2026, and could override conflicting measures on this ballot if it receives more Yes votes.

contests.title: Proposition 43 — Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services
contests.shortTitle: A two-thirds vote for local special taxes
contests.summary: Starting January 1, 2027, requires a two-thirds vote instead of a majority for voter-proposed local special taxes, including new taxes, increases and extensions.

contests.title: Proposition 44 — Requires Community Health Clinics Spend 90% of Revenue on Program Services
contests.summary: Requires covered nonprofit community health clinics to spend at least 90% of annual revenue on services advancing their charitable purpose. It adds penalties and reporting rules, with temporary waivers possible for exceptional circumstances or financial hardship.

contests.title: Proposition 45 — Modifies Environmental Review for Certain Projects
contests.summary: Lets applicants for qualifying housing, infrastructure and other projects choose new environmental-review procedures with tighter agency and court deadlines. These procedures also limit project alternatives, public-comment periods, and the scope of court challenges and remedies.
